newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Globale Kranken says to double premiums.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Globale Kranken says to double premiums.

text.p: German private health insurer Globale Krankenversicherungs-AG (GLK), which is controlled by Deutsche Bank, plans to double its premium income within two years, said Karl-Peter Thevessen, chairman of the management board.

For 1996 GLK expects premium income of 55-60 million marks. The aim for 1998 is to achieve premium income of 100 million marks. "Thanks to the sales channels of our shareholders we can manage such leaps in premium volume. There are still enormous possibilities."
GLK started business in late 1993 and is 55 percent owned by Deutsche Bank and 45 percent by Gerling.

In 1995, the company had gross premium income of 33.1 million marks, while claims amounted to 13.0 million marks. After costs, GLK recorded a 13.7 million marks deficit, covered by its parent companies.
Thevessen expects that the deficit will be reduced in 1996 and 1997 and that break-even will be reached by 1998. "All in all the setting-up of the company will cost 50 million marks," he said.

At the moment, GLK has 8,500 full medical expenses policies in its portfolio. The company currently suffers from a high cancellation ratio. It loses about 25 percent of its new business, mainly due to insolvencies or to insureds whose income drops below the ceiling under which statutory health cover becomes obligatory again.
In 1997 GLK will thus concentrate on measures to consolidate the portfolio and to improve its service.
Another focus of activity will be the market for complementary cover for people who are insured within the state health system.

Thevessen is convinced that the private health market in Germany will soon bottom out. "If no major political changes occur, we will in the medium term have a considerably better growth potential compared with the state system."

Thevessen believes that German employers should be obliged by law to participate in deductibles their employees pay in private health insurance. Then private health insurance tariffs with deductibles could be sold more widely and allow better control of cost development.

Employers in Germany currently have to pay 50 percent of the employee's premium for private health cover. If the insured votes for a high deductible -- which considerably reduces the premium -- he has to pay alone for that in most cases.
